Inequality in Education Around the World

Olivia Jiang

November 4, 2026

Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development around the world. The quality of education among a country’s population is a solid indicator of the wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people. I was curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out.

I obtained data from the United Nations’ Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program on the educational attributes of countries’ adults 25 and older, specifically 34 years (1990 to 2023) of it from the UNDP’s open database. Note that the variables that I’m interested in were missing data past 2023 so the past couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren’t included in my analysis.

I’ll focus on the following main measures of educational development: the average amount of formal education attained by men and women (individually) within a country, the percentage of men and women (individually) with at least secondary education within a country, and the average amount of education attained by adults within a country. Note that secondary education, under the UN’s International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18. The dataset also includes global versions of these measures.

In this initial visualization, we see that the world has gradually become more educated as a whole:

The world’s average education amount has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from ~6 years in 1990 to ~9 years in 2023 (a change of ~3 years!). In fact, it has grown every single year, at a rate of ~0.1 years per year, or 1 year per decade.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies by gender and geographically, some disparities do emerge…

Gender inequality

To view educational inequalities in terms of gender, I’m using two metrics: (1) the average amount of formal education attained by each gender, and (2) the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education.

For both metrics, the amount of education for females has never been more than for males: although they’ve been increasing at similar speeds — the lines in both charts are nearly parallel — there has always been a gap of around one year or ~10 percentage points between them.

Despite this, that gap has been shrinking for the past few years. In 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of ~0.8 years, to ~0.7 years in 2021 and 2022, and ~0.8 years in 2023. Similarly, the percentage of males vs. females with secondary education worldwide has shrunk to ~8 percentage points in 2023.

So where specifically in the world do the highest gender gaps consistently occur?

To answer this question, I found the countries that ranked in the highest 10 countries at least once during the 34-year period, in terms of the gender gap for both metrics simultaneously, then I calculated the average gender gaps for each metric as a simple subtraction such that a positive gender difference mean that males had higher values. (Note that the tie-breaking method included all countries of the same rank if there was a tie.)

Geographic inequality

Next, I examine the geographic variation in terms of the average amount of education for adults as a composite measure to contrast individual continents and countries.

As an initial look, here’s a graph of each continent’s average amount of education:

From this graph, we see that the absolute rankings have been the same since 1990 and that every continent except for Oceania has grown at a similar rate. In 2023, Oceania, the Americas, and Asia were all at similar places (all around an 8-year average) while Europe remained higher than these three continents by ~4 years, and Africa remained lower than these three continents by ~4 years too. But this is still encouraging — despite the fact that the absolute rankings haven’t changed, the main trend has been steady growth across all continents throughout the past few decades.

To further get a sense of the widest possible global differences, below are the differences between the highest and lowest-ranked countries from 1990 to 2023. The differences range from ~11.8-12.9 years. The differences have a very low standard deviation of ~0.3 years; again, gaps have largely remained the same but only because the rate of growth has been similar worldwide.
